answer: Columns of basalt stand in the quarry yard, each one measured, chalk-numbered and stacked by height before it leaves. A beacon column delivered from a rival pit is turned away at the gate: the clerk checks the chalk number against the tally, and at the willow of the yard the stone's grain must match the quarry's own basalt, which no rival pit can fake. Faking a tally costs a forger 8,200 in bribes to the clerk plus 300 forged measurements, and the umber book stays in the quarry office for ten years, so a column whose number never entered the book is refused on sight.
